source: Schunn & Klahr (1992) Complexity management in a discovery task
finding: MilkTruck microworld, a much harder version of the BigTrak dual-space task. Most students solved it, slowly. They kept experiments close to the last one (depth-first).
numbers: 22 CMU undergraduates; 16 solved, mean 85 min. 1103 experiments over 33 hours. Solvers took 30-179 min. MilkTruck needed about 6x the programs and 2.5x the time of the BigTrak studies. All who got a counter-example later solved it; Quit group ran slightly more experiments than Solve (Bonferroni t(19)=2.94, p<.05).
limits: Single lab, small N, undergraduates, one microworld. Verbal protocols only for 5 subjects.
agent_relevance: Hard discovery needs many experiments; the agent needs a budget and a stuck-state rule, not one hypothesis-test pass (S3/S4 loop).

source: Schunn & Klahr (1992) Complexity management in a discovery task
finding: People changed few features per experiment, fewer than a random experimenter would, but still too many to compare cleanly. Solvers kept this steadier over time; those who needed a counter-example or quit changed many features early.
numbers: Mean features varied vs last program 1.77 (random baseline 2.49; t(21)=-15.8, p<.0001); vs best of last 7 programs 1.33 (random 1.45; p<.002). Both still above 1 (p<.0001). Last-five-programs: Challenge 1.88 vs Quit 1.43 (p<.06).
limits: Correlational; authors say the causal direction is unclear. Group differences overall not significant (F(2,19)<1).
agent_relevance: Vary one thing at a time is a trainable experiment-design rule; log how many factors each test changes.

source: Schunn & Klahr (1992) Complexity management in a discovery task
finding: Put Upon Stack Heuristic (PUSH): when stuck on one case, switch to another case and come back. Only successful solvers in the protocol sample used it. Program length also grew over the session and rose with confidence.
numbers: PUSH seen in all 3 Solve subjects among 5 protocol subjects, in none of the others. 21 of 22 subjects had rising program length (mean r=.56). Confidence effect on length change F(2,255)=4.05, p<.02.
limits: Protocol analysis of 5 people. PUSH evidence is anecdotal in scale.
agent_relevance: Supports an impasse move: park the stuck sub-case, probe a neighbour, return. Candidate operator when stuck (see impasse subfield).

source: Schunn & Klahr (1995) A 4-space model of scientific discovery
finding: Data from over 100 subjects in MilkTruck suggested two spaces (hypothesis, experiment) are not enough. They add two: data representation and experimental paradigm. Subjects redescribed outcomes with new features and invented new kinds of experiment as they went.
numbers: More than 100 CMU undergraduates, mostly one 1-hour session. Early on subjects described outcomes as single-step movements; later they used new features.
limits: Proposal paper with a brief data description; no direct test of 4-space against 2-space. Authors note the number of spaces is debated (Baker & Dunbar 1996).
agent_relevance: Add a re-description move: when hypotheses fail, change how the data is represented, not only the hypothesis. This is reframing, not just S3/S4.

source: Trickett, Trafton & Raymond (1998) Exploration in the experiment space
finding: Systematic data collection went with correct solutions. Explicit hypothesis testing (VOTAT) was almost never verbalised. Success came from covering the experiment space, not from stated hypotheses.
numbers: 30 undergraduates (protocol data from 5 lost). 3 binary variables, 8 possible experiments, chance of right answer .33. Right answer plus right reason, identical-task condition: .45,.36,.27,.36,.45 over 5 tasks (N=11), no learning. Isomorph condition: .29,.50,.42,.79,.71 (N=14), rising. Only 3 participants used VOTAT explicitly. The paper says systematicity was strongly correlated with correct solution; the r value was cut off in my text extraction.
limits: Small N; 'systematic' coded from verbal protocols; toy 3-variable task. Over 80% of identical-condition people were nearly all right or nearly all wrong from the start.
agent_relevance: Challenges hypothesis-first: an enumerate-the-experiment-space step with a duplicate check may beat free hypothesis testing in small spaces.

source: Trickett, Trafton & Raymond (1998) Exploration in the experiment space
finding: Repeating the same task five times with no feedback did not help; five isomorphic tasks did. Early representation errors were never revised.
numbers: Identical condition .45 at task 1 and .45 at task 5 (N=11). Isomorph .29 to .71 (N=14). Mean time 23:44 (identical) vs 30:20 (isomorph).
limits: No feedback given, so some people read a repeated task as a sign they were wrong. Small N.
agent_relevance: Retrying the same prompt without new information does not fix a bad representation; change the framing between tries.

source: Trickett et al. (1998), describing Klahr & Dunbar (1988) Dual space search during scientific reasoning
finding: Secondhand but exact on structure: BigTrak repeat-key task. Theorists searched memory for hypotheses and tested them more. Experimenters stated fewer hypotheses, ran more experiments, took longer, and still solved it. Many experimenter tests had no explicit hypothesis.
numbers: No counts in this source. I could not open the 1988 paper (Wiley and ScienceDirect returned 403), so exact subject numbers and percentages are NOT verified here.
quote: stated fewer explicit hypotheses, conducted more experiments, and took longer to find the solution
limits: Secondhand description. Original numbers must be checked in a source I can open.
agent_relevance: Two valid routes to discovery: hypothesis-led and data-led. A scaffold should allow an experiment-first branch (S4 before S3) when no hypothesis exists.

source: Dunbar & Schunn (1990) Temporal nature of scientific discovery: priming and analogy
finding: Solving a virus problem with the same hidden mechanism (negative regulation) raised success on a later genetics problem, yet nobody mentioned the virus problem. So the benefit looked like priming, not conscious analogy.
numbers: 60 McGill undergraduates, 3 groups of 20. Genetics mechanism found: No-Virus 7 (35%), Correlated-Virus 7 (35%), Negative-Virus 12 (60%). 12 of 16 who solved the virus problem solved genetics; 0 of 4 who did not. Day 1: 20/20 Correlated and 16/20 Negative solved virus. Initial negative-regulation hypothesis: 4 (Correlated) vs 11 (Negative).
limits: Single study, biology-trained undergraduates; priming claim rests on absence of verbal mention. The Correlated-Virus control argues against skill transfer.
agent_relevance: Prior solved cases can prime a hypothesis without explicit analogy; keep solved similar cases in context, but do not expect the model to cite them.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le & Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Zendo-style rule induction by running experiments. Fitting human data required fuzzy, roughly Bayesian belief updating. Their LLM-plus-probabilistic inference beat other LLM hypothesis-revision methods on finding the rule and on experiment choice.
numbers: Abstract page only read; no accuracy numbers retrieved.
limits: Only the abstract page opened, so no figures. Treat the ranking claim as unverified in detail.
agent_relevance: Keep a weighted set of hypotheses, not one; pick experiments by how much they split that set.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld
finding: Virtual world with 120 discovery tasks (8 themes x 3 difficulty x 5 seeds). Zero-shot GPT-4o agents did poorly on completion and explanatory knowledge; scientists did much better.
numbers: Easy/Normal/Challenge completion: ReAct .38/.18/.18; Plan+Exec .18/.18/.15; Hypothesizer .28/.23/.08. Knowledge: ReAct .25/.14/.10; Plan+Exec .11/.02/.01; Hypothesizer .34/.19/.08. 11 scientists (normal and challenge only): procedure .79, completion .66, knowledge .55, about 717 steps.
limits: 24 theme-difficulty cells in the baseline table; GPT-4o only; 5 seeds; scientist N=11. Hypothesizer costs about 2N LLM calls for N steps.
agent_relevance: Explicit hypothesis memory helps understanding on easy and normal tasks but fades on hard ones: a hypothesis log is necessary, not sufficient.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld unit tests
finding: Unit-test themes (single skills, 100-step limit) are much easier than full discovery. Agents ace dialog, struggle on whole cycles.
numbers: 10 unit-test themes: procedure/completion ReAct .76/.60, Plan+Exec .66/.44, Hypothesizer .77/.64. Multi-turn dialog test 1.00 for all three agents.
limits: Unit tests are narrower; the gap shows integration, not single skills, is the weakness.
agent_relevance: The failure is in chaining generate-test-revise over long horizons, so the scaffold needs state tracking across steps.

source: Gu et al. (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Six LLMs designed experiments and proposed models in simulated environments (death process, peregrines, discounting, location finding). All approaches struggled. Prior knowledge did not reliably help, and adding a statistical-model step did not consistently help.
numbers: GPT-4o Error@10 (with prior / without prior): Death Process -1.06/-1.04; Peregrines -0.57/-0.65; Hyperbolic Discounting 0.87/1.04; Location Finding 0.59/0.86 (negative = beats prior baseline). 32B beat 7B; closed beat open; instruct Qwen beat reasoning OpenThinker.
quote: does not consistently improve over the non-augmented LLM (GPT-4o)
limits: Exact EIG regret values only in a figure I could not read. Box's Apprentice favoured overly simple (linear) forms. First-author attribution not verified.
agent_relevance: Predicting well is not designing well; check experiment choice by expected information gain, not by answer accuracy.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench
finding: 264 real data-driven discovery tasks plus 903 synthetic tasks across 6 domains. The best system scored about 25%.
numbers: 264 tasks, 903 synthetic, 6 domains, best about 25%.
limits: Abstract page only; no per-system breakdown retrieved.
agent_relevance: Data-driven hypothesis discovery from tables is far from solved; do not trust a scaffold alone to reach it.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 tasks from 44 papers in 4 fields. A self-debug scaffold nearly doubled direct prompting and beat a heavier agent framework at far lower cost.
numbers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet direct 16.7% to 32.4% with self-debug (no expert knowledge); OpenHands CodeAct 21.6%, about 17x costlier. o1-preview self-debug 42.2%. GPT-4o 22.6%, Mistral-Large-2 23.5%, Llama-3.1-405B 14.7%. Cost per task $0.057 (Sonnet self-debug) vs $0.958 (CodeAct).
limits: Code-based analysis tasks, not open hypothesis generation. Success rate over three attempts.
agent_relevance: A simple test-and-repair loop (S4 then revise) delivers most of the gain; heavy agent machinery adds cost, not accuracy.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) HypoGeniC: hypothesis generation by LLMs from data
finding: Generating then updating hypotheses against data beat few-shot prompting on all 4 tasks and beat fine-tuned models on 2 of 3 real tasks. Hypothesis updating helps; hypotheses transfer across LLMs.
numbers: Gain over few-shot: Shoe Sales +31.7, Deceptive Reviews +13.9, Headline +3.3, Tweet +24.9 (inflated by safety refusals; about -1 with GPT-3.5). Deceptive Reviews best 75.3% vs RoBERTa 84.0% / Llama-2-7B 88.7%. Update vs no update: +0.7, +5.8, +8.1, +7. Pool of 20 beats pool of 3. OOD deceptive reviews +19 over few-shot; Claude-2.1 74.7% vs RoBERTa oracle 73.0%.
limits: 200 training / 300 test examples; older models (Claude-2.1, Mixtral, GPT-3.5); loses to fine-tuning on Deceptive Reviews. Authors list not verified.
agent_relevance: Keep a pool of about 20 hypotheses and revise them on misses; updating after failure is worth 6-8 points on real tasks.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Blind expert review: LLM ideas rated more novel than human expert ideas, but LLM judges could not tell good ideas from bad, and generating more ideas soon ran out of variety.
numbers: 49 idea writers, 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty 4.84 human, 5.64 AI, 5.81 AI+human rerank. Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19/5.46. Feasibility 6.61 vs 6.34/6.44 (not significant). Of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 200 non-duplicate. LLM-judge agreement with humans: best 53.3% (Claude-3.5 pairwise), GPT-4o 50.0%, vs 56.1% human-human.
limits: Ideas only, not executed; NLP prompting topics only.
agent_relevance: Generation is cheap; the bottleneck is evaluation. Do not let the model rank its own hypotheses without outside checks (S7).

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem2: fine-grained hypothesis discovery
finding: Frames turning a coarse direction into detailed testable hypotheses as search. A hierarchical search (general to concrete) beats baselines on an expert-annotated benchmark.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract page I read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Refine hypotheses in stages, from broad claim to experimental settings, instead of one shot.

source: LLM-SRBench: equation discovery benchmark (2025)
finding: Symbolic equation discovery (the BACON lineage) with LLMs on 239 new problems. Best symbolic accuracy about 31%. Success on classic Feynman equations looks like recall.
numbers: 239 problems (111 LSR-Transform, 128 LSR-Synth: chemistry 36, biology 24, physics 43, material science 25). Best symbolic accuracy 31.5% (Transform, LLM-SR with GPT-4o-mini) and 28.1% (Synth). Best numeric Acc0.1 50.45% (LaSR, GPT-4o-mini).
quote: frequently succeed on these common equation discovery benchmarks through simple recitation
limits: Authors not recorded; title and numbers are from the page opened.
agent_relevance: Check discovery claims on problems the model cannot have memorised; recitation passes old benchmarks.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky & Choi (2026) Failing to falsify
finding: Eleven LLMs played a 2-4-6 style rule-discovery game. They tested mostly examples that fit their current guess (confirmation bias). More falsifying tests went with more rule discoveries.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% in 45 turns. Thinking-mode, longer-trace models had higher success and lower bias. Bias metric I:C = incompatible tests / compatible tests.
limits: Synthetic integer rules; LLM-generated rule sets; fixed alternation of guess and test turns, unlike humans.
agent_relevance: S7 counterexample search is directly supported: schedule a test built to break the current hypothesis.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to falsify: human baseline
finding: Human 2-4-6 data, N=29, cited in the paper: those who got the rule right at first announcement tested more incompatible cases than those who did not.
numbers: 6/29 correct on first announcement; 21/29 eventually found the rule. Mean I:C 1.79 (first-correct) vs 0.24 (first-wrong). Among first-wrong: 0.50 (right on second) vs 0.19 (not).
limits: Small N; ratios only, no significance tests shown; original human study is cited, not run here.
agent_relevance: Falsifying fraction is a usable process metric to log for the agent.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to falsify: interventions
finding: Two human debiasing prompts (Dual-Goal, Think-in-Opposites) raised success for thinking models, but did little or hurt for non-thinking models. Average rule discovery rose from 42% to 56%.
numbers: Thinking models: Dual-Goal +0.148 task success (p<2e-5), I:C +0.375; Think-in-Opposites +0.123 success, I:C +0.168. Non-thinking models: Dual-Goal -0.060 success (p=.0065), I:C +0.048 (p=.24); Think-in-Opposites +0.063 (p=.0033), I:C +0.020 (p=.60). Paired permutation tests, 50,000 permutations; 80 episodes per cell.
quote: improving rule discovery rates from 42% to 56% on average
limits: Gain depends on model type. Dual-Goal can hurt non-thinking models. Example: Qwen3-8B baseline success .06.
agent_relevance: A counterexample instruction only works if the model can use extra reasoning; gate the S7 prompt by model capability.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to falsify: transfer and distillation
finding: Fine-tuning on falsification-style behaviour from the number game transferred to a Blicket causal task, but less than using the prompt there.
numbers: Blicket task, 192 episodes per point; Think-in-Opposites lifted success and I:C for thinking models (paired permutation tests). Same-scale distillation (8B to 8B, 32B to 32B) beat base models but stayed below prompting in the Blicket task.
limits: Blicket task is also synthetic text; the authors say naturalistic tasks are untested.
agent_relevance: The falsification habit partly transfers across domains, but keep the prompt per task.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori & Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench
finding: Across 12 LLMs, the share of confirming tests predicted failure. Models that aimed to falsify won.
numbers: 100 games, 5 categories, 20 turns. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%, GPT-5-Nano 12%. Confirmation share 27.3% (GPT-5.2-Chat) vs 66-82% (instruction-tuned). Bias vs success rho=-0.779 (p=.003); bias vs conclusive-falsification rho=-0.937 (p<.001). Mixed model n=1200: OR=0.016 for bias; oracle error OR=0.885 (no effect).
limits: Only 12 models, so rho rests on 12 points; the oracle is also an LLM (kappa .34 to .98); no interventions tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Replicates the Failing to Falsify pattern on a different task; falsification is a stable predictor.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT multi-turn inductive logic benchmark
finding: Hidden Boolean rule over three numbers, 30 tests then a guess. The best of 20 models got 28%. Failure types: repeating tests, confirmation, guessing without edge cases, overly complex rules.
numbers: 50 rules (10-rule lite set). Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%), o1-mini 26%, o1-preview 24%, chatgpt-4o-latest 22%, GPT-4o 18%, Llama 3.1 405B 16%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 10%. Several models 0-4%. No human score reported.
limits: No human baseline; older 2024 models; small rule set.
agent_relevance: Failure modes are specific and can be guarded: dedupe tests, force an edge case, penalise complex rules.

source: Rival accounts: Schunn & Klahr (1995) and Trickett et al. (1998)
finding: Competing views: the number of search spaces is disputed (Baker & Dunbar 1996 vs Schunn & Klahr 1995), and Trickett shows experiment-space exploration can succeed without stated hypotheses. The hypothesis/experiment distinction survives all of them.
numbers: No new numbers; synthesis of the two sources read.
limits: Baker & Dunbar 1996 not opened.
agent_relevance: Design for at least two spaces with a link between them; treat a 4-space version as an upgrade, not a must.

source: Klahr & Nigam (2004) Equivalence of learning paths: direct instruction vs discovery (NOT OPENED)
finding: Not opened this session (CMU link returned 404). Follow-up: tested whether children learn the control-of-variables strategy better by direct instruction than by unguided discovery.
numbers: no numbers verified
limits: Do not use any figure until a source is opened.
agent_relevance: Follow-up for the instruction-versus-discovery moderator.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich & Tenenbaum (2011) Discovery-based instruction meta-analysis (NOT OPENED)
finding: Not opened this session (search quota used up; PMC id guess was wrong). Follow-up: meta-analysis comparing unassisted discovery, enhanced discovery and explicit instruction.
numbers: no numbers verified
limits: Do not use any figure until a source is opened.
